title: How TSMC Uses Old Fabs to Make New Chips
gist: A short (~255 word) forum post with unusually specific operational detail: TSMC is meeting AI-chip demand through 'cross-node utilization' — roughly 90 percent tool overlap across successive nodes lets it start N3/N5 critical layers in Tainan, truck partly-finished wafers to underutilized N7/N6 fabs in Taichung for later steps, and add effective leading-edge capacity without waiting the ~2 years for 2026-funded fabs to deliver in 2028.

insights.claim: TSMC has reported roughly 90 percent tool overlap among several successive process nodes, meaning nodes are not separate manufacturing systems and capacity can be converted or shared as customers migrate between processes.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A 90% overlap figure means TSMC's effective leading-edge capacity is materially larger than nameplate node capacity — models based on node-specific wafer starts understate supply.
insights.quote: TSMC has reported roughly 90 percent tool overlap among several successive nodes.

insights.claim: Many production steps — especially the upper interconnect layers — use similar recipes and tools across adjacent nodes, which is the physical basis for shifting work between older and newer fabs.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Back-end-of-line commonality, not front-end lithography, is where fungible capacity lives — the layer to examine when assessing any foundry's flexibility.
insights.locator: Process nodes are not separate manufacturing systems

insights.claim: TSMC reserves its advanced Tainan facilities for the most technically demanding N3 and N5 layers, then trucks unfinished wafers to less-utilized N7/N6 facilities in Taichung where compatible equipment completes the later, less critical steps.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Explains how N3 output can rise faster than N3 tool installs — a specific, checkable mechanism behind TSMC upside surprises on advanced-node revenue.
insights.quote: then transport unfinished wafers by truck to less-utilized N7/N6 facilities in Taichung, where compatible equipment completes later, less critical steps
insights.locator: TSMC can reserve its advanced facilities in Tainan

insights.claim: New fab capacity funded in 2026 may not reach customers until 2028, so incremental near-term AI-chip supply must come from squeezing more output from existing factories and equipment rather than from new construction.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: A ~2-year capex-to-output lag means 2026 capex announcements are irrelevant to 2026-27 supply; near-term AI chip scarcity is resolved by utilization tricks, not capex.
insights.quote: New capacity funded in 2026 may not reach customers until 2028
insights.locator: TSMC’s answer to soaring AI-chip demand

insights.claim: Nvidia and other customers need N3 capacity while N5 remains busy and newer fabs take years to complete, making cross-node flexibility the binding constraint on near-term AI accelerator supply.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Watch N3 allocation and N7/N6 utilization together — rising N7/N6 loading may signal N3 throughput expansion rather than a mature-node demand recovery.
insights.locator: AI demand makes this flexibility valuable

insights.claim: Cross-node capacity sharing reduces the risk that multibillion-dollar fabs become stranded or underused as customers migrate to newer processes, effectively extending the economic life of older facilities.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Lower stranded-asset risk supports TSMC's return on invested capital versus peers whose older nodes go idle — a structural margin argument, not a cyclical one.
insights.locator: reducing the risk that multibillion-dollar fabs become stranded

themes.theme: Island-wide production pool as competitive moat

insights.claim: An inter-fab trucking network links geographically separated TSMC fabs into a flexible, island-wide production pool that lets capacity follow demand — turning Taiwan's geographic concentration into an operational advantage.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: This advantage cannot be replicated at dispersed overseas fabs (Arizona, Kumamoto, Dresden) — a concrete reason overseas TSMC capacity is structurally less efficient.
insights.quote: It links separated fabs into a flexible, island-wide production pool, allowing capacity to follow demand

insights.claim: The cross-node wafer-shuttling approach is explicitly temporary and carries conversion costs, so it is a bridge to new capacity rather than a permanent operating model.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Caps how long this supply-side relief lasts; if AI demand persists past 2028 the constraint reverts to physical fab construction schedules.
insights.quote: The approach is temporary and carries conversion costs

insights.claim: TSMC's distinctive advantage is the combination of a Taiwanese manufacturing base, large installed capacity and enough process commonality to scale AI-chip output faster than construction alone would permit — three factors that must co-exist and that competitors lack in combination.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Intel Foundry and Samsung cannot match this without both scale and dense geographic clustering — reinforces TSMC share durability in AI logic through the current cycle.
insights.quote: a Taiwanese manufacturing base, installed capacity, and enough process commonality to scale AI-chip output faster than construction alone would permit
